question: What is light?
teaser: See an atom give out one colour of light, meet the particle of light, and watch what the eye does with it.

stops.title: Sunlight
text: Sunlight lights the park and warms the grass. It also carries information: everything you see, you see by light that bounced off it or came from it.
What is that light made of?
stops.notice: Look at the shadows. Light travels in straight lines until something blocks it.

stops.title: An atom gives out one colour
text: A hydrogen atom has one electron, and the electron can only have certain amounts of energy. When it drops from a higher energy to a lower one, the atom gives out a single packet of light.
The bigger the drop, the bluer the light. The drop from the third level to the second gives the red line of hydrogen, at a wavelength of about 656 nanometres.
stops.model: Bohr's 1913 picture, with the electron on circles, is a simple model that works for hydrogen but fails for atoms with more electrons. The real atom is the cloud in the quantum view.
stops.notice: Press the button that makes the electron jump, and watch the packet of light leave.

stops.title: The particle of light
text: A packet of light is called a photon. It has no mass and no electric charge, and it always moves at the speed of light.
Sunlight is a stream of photons, and so are radio waves and X-rays, only with different energies. Photons are also what carries the electric and magnetic forces between charged particles.
stops.model: A map of the particles. Positions are a diagram, and the sizes mean nothing.
stops.notice: Find the photon in the group of force carriers.

stops.title: The eye catches photons
text: The eye focuses light onto the retina at the back, which has about 120 million rods and about 6 million cones. Cones give colour and fine detail in bright light, and there are three kinds.
Each light-sensing cell can respond when its pigment absorbs a photon.
stops.notice: Look at the layers at the back of the eye cut open.

stops.title: A molecule that changes shape
text: This is retinal, the light-sensitive part of the visual pigment in your eye. When it absorbs a photon, the molecule changes shape.
That change starts a chain of signals that ends in a nerve impulse to your brain, and you see.
stops.model: A computed shape of one retinal molecule, at true size.
stops.notice: Look at the long chain of alternating bonds. That chain is what lets the molecule take in visible light.

answer: Light is a stream of photons, packets of energy with no mass that atoms give out when an electron drops to a lower level and that molecules in your eye take in.
unknown: Light behaves as a wave in some experiments and as particles in others. The theory that unites the two, quantum electrodynamics, is one of the best tested in science, but what the "particle" is, beyond what the equations say, is still argued about.
